subject: Biology
title: Concept and Classification of Living Things
outline: Distinguish living things from non-living things using the seven characteristics of life (MR NIGER D)
Explain the concept of the cell as the basic unit of life and the levels of biological organisation
Describe the classification hierarchy from kingdom to species
Apply the rules of binomial nomenclature correctly
Compare the general features of the five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia
Use simple dichotomous keys to identify organisms

modules.title: Characteristics of Living Things and Levels of Organisation
modules.html:
1. What is Biology?

Biology is the scientific study of living things (organisms), their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution, distribution and interactions with one another and with their environment. It branches broadly into botany (plants), zoology (animals) and microbiology (micro-organisms).

2. The Seven Characteristics of Life

The mnemonic MR NIGER D summarises the life processes shown by all living organisms:

  1. Movement – change in position of the whole body (locomotion in animals) or of a part (tropic and nastic movements in plants).
  2. Respiration – the controlled release of energy from food within cells.
  3. Nutrition – taking in and using materials for energy, growth and repair; autotrophic in green plants, heterotrophic in animals and fungi.
  4. Irritability (sensitivity) – detecting and responding to stimuli such as light, heat, gravity, water and chemicals.
  5. Growth – permanent, irreversible increase in size, mass and complexity by cell division and assimilation.
  6. Excretion – removal of toxic metabolic wastes (urea, carbon dioxide, excess salts).
  7. Reproduction – production of new individuals, sexually or asexually, to continue the species.
  8. Death – the irreversible end of all life processes; all living things eventually die, non-living things do not.

3. Living, Non-living and Once-living

FeatureLiving thingsNon-living things
Cellular structureMade of cells with protoplasmNo cells or protoplasm
GrowthInternal (intussusception)External accretion only (e.g. crystals)
EnergyRespire to release energyDo not respire
ResponseSensitive to stimuliNot sensitive
Life spanDefinite; ends in deathIndefinite

Viruses occupy a borderline position: they possess nucleic acid and can reproduce, but only inside a living host cell, and they can be crystallised like chemicals.

4. Levels of Biological Organisation

Complexity increases in a clear sequence:

  • Cell – basic structural and functional unit (e.g. Amoeba, red blood cell).
  • Tissue – similar cells performing one function (xylem, muscle).
  • Organ – several tissues working together (leaf, heart).
  • System – organs cooperating (digestive system, shoot system).
  • Organism – the complete individual.
  • Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biosphere – ecological levels.

Organisms may be unicellular (Paramecium), colonial (Volvox), filamentous (Spirogyra) or multicellular with division of labour (mammals, flowering plants).

examples.q: A car burns petrol, moves and gives out exhaust gases. Why is it not classified as a living thing?
examples.a: Although it appears to 'move', 'respire' and 'excrete', a car is not made of cells, cannot grow from within, cannot reproduce itself and is not sensitive to stimuli in a coordinated way. Life is defined by the possession of all the characteristics of MR NIGER D within a cellular, protoplasmic body.

examples.q: Arrange in increasing order of complexity: organ, cell, organism, tissue, system.
examples.a: Cell → tissue → organ → system → organism. For example: palisade cell → palisade mesophyll tissue → leaf → shoot system → mango tree.

modules.title: Classification and Binomial Nomenclature
modules.html:
1. Why Classify?

Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing and grouping organisms. Classification (i) makes the study of about two million known species manageable, (ii) shows evolutionary relationships, (iii) allows accurate international communication, and (iv) helps in identification of new organisms.

2. The Taxonomic Hierarchy

From the largest, most inclusive group to the smallest:

  1. Kingdom
  2. Phylum (Division in plants)
  3. Class
  4. Order
  5. Family
  6. Genus
  7. Species

Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup. As we descend the hierarchy the number of organisms per group decreases while the number of shared characteristics increases.

3. The Species Concept

A species is a group of organisms with very similar features that can interbreed freely to produce fertile offspring. A horse (Equus caballus) crossed with a donkey (Equus asinus) gives a mule, which is sterile — proof that they are separate species.

4. Rules of Binomial Nomenclature (Linnaeus, 1753)

  • Every organism has a two-word Latin name: generic name + specific epithet.
  • The generic name begins with a capital letter; the specific epithet is entirely lower case: Homo sapiens, Zea mays.
  • The name is printed in italics and underlined separately when handwritten.
  • After first mention the genus may be abbreviated: E. coli.

5. Dichotomous Keys

A dichotomous key presents paired, contrasting statements; at each step the user chooses one and is directed onward until the organism is named. Example:

  1. a. Body with jointed legs … go to 2
    b. Body without jointed legs … earthworm
  2. a. Three pairs of legs … insect
    b. Four pairs of legs … spider

examples.q: Write the scientific name of maize correctly and identify the parts.
examples.a: Zea mays — Zea is the generic name (capital initial) and mays is the specific epithet (small letter). Both are italicised in print and underlined separately in handwriting.

examples.q: Two organisms belong to the same family but different genera. Which taxa do they certainly share?
examples.a: They share kingdom, phylum, class, order and family, but differ from genus downwards. Shared characteristics therefore exist at the family level and above.

modules.title: The Five Kingdoms
modules.html:
Whittaker’s Five-Kingdom Scheme (1969)

KingdomCell typeBodyNutritionExamples
MoneraProkaryotic (no true nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles)UnicellularAutotrophic or heterotrophicBacteria, cyanobacteria (Nostoc)
ProtistaEukaryoticMostly unicellularPhotosynthetic or holozoicAmoeba, Paramecium, Euglena, Plasmodium
FungiEukaryotic, chitin wallHyphae forming myceliumSaprophytic or parasitic (heterotrophic, no chlorophyll)Rhizopus, mushroom, yeast
PlantaeEukaryotic, cellulose wallMulticellularAutotrophic (photosynthesis)Mosses, ferns, maize, mango
AnimaliaEukaryotic, no cell wallMulticellularHeterotrophic (holozoic)Insects, fish, birds, humans

Major Plant Divisions

  • Thallophyta – algae; simple thallus.
  • Bryophyta – mosses and liverworts; no vascular tissue, need water for fertilisation.
  • Pteridophyta – ferns; vascular but seedless, reproduce by spores.
  • Spermatophyta – seed plants: Gymnospermae (naked seeds, e.g. Cycas) and Angiospermae (seeds in fruits; monocots vs dicots).

Major Animal Phyla

  • Porifera (sponges), Coelenterata (Hydra, jellyfish), Platyhelminthes (tapeworm), Nematoda (Ascaris), Annelida (earthworm), Mollusca (snail), Arthropoda (insects, crustaceans, arachnids, myriapods), Echinodermata (starfish), Chordata (fish, amphibia, reptiles, birds, mammals).

Arthropoda is the largest phylum; its members have an exoskeleton of chitin, jointed appendages, a segmented body and open circulation.

examples.q: Euglena shows both plant and animal features. Explain and state its kingdom.
examples.a: It has chloroplasts and photosynthesises (plant-like) but also possesses a flagellum for locomotion, an eyespot and a contractile vacuole, and can feed heterotrophically in darkness (animal-like). Because it is a unicellular eukaryote it is placed in the kingdom Protista.

examples.q: Why are fungi no longer classified as plants?
examples.a: Fungi lack chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise; their cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose; they store glycogen rather than starch and feed saprophytically or parasitically by extracellular digestion. These differences justify a separate kingdom.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of living things?
quiz.solution: Crystallisation is a physical property of non-living substances such as salt; it is not a life process.

quiz.q: The mnemonic MR NIGER D is used to remember the
quiz.solution: MR NIGER D stands for Movement, Respiration, Nutrition, Irritability, Growth, Excretion, Reproduction and Death.

quiz.q: Growth in living organisms differs from 'growth' in crystals because living growth is
quiz.solution: Living organisms grow by intussusception — new material is added inside the body and the increase is permanent and irreversible.

quiz.q: The correct sequence of increasing complexity is
quiz.solution: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs cooperate as systems.

quiz.q: Which organism is a colonial protist showing early division of labour?
quiz.solution: Volvox forms a hollow spherical colony of flagellated cells with some cells specialised for reproduction.

quiz.q: The scientific name of the domestic cat is written correctly as
quiz.solution: The generic name takes a capital initial and the specific epithet a small letter; the whole name is italicised.

quiz.q: Which taxon contains the largest number of different organisms?
quiz.solution: Kingdom is the widest taxon; as one moves down the hierarchy the group becomes smaller and more specific.

quiz.q: Members of the same species are best defined by their ability to
quiz.solution: Reproductive compatibility yielding fertile offspring is the biological species criterion; a mule is sterile, so horse and donkey are separate species.

quiz.q: Organisms in the kingdom Monera are characterised by
options: the absence of a nuclear membrane
quiz.solution: Monerans are prokaryotes: their genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm without a nuclear membrane.

quiz.q: The cell wall of fungi is composed mainly of
quiz.solution: Fungal walls contain chitin, unlike the cellulose walls of plants.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a seedless vascular plant?
quiz.solution: Ferns (Pteridophyta) possess xylem and phloem but reproduce by spores, not seeds.

quiz.q: A distinguishing feature of phylum Arthropoda is the possession of
options: a soft body with a mantle
quiz.solution: Jointed limbs plus a chitinous exoskeleton define arthropods; tube feet belong to echinoderms and the mantle to molluscs.

quiz.q: Viruses are difficult to classify mainly because they
options: can be crystallised and reproduce only inside host cells
quiz.solution: Their ability to be crystallised (non-living trait) and their obligate intracellular reproduction (living trait) place them on the borderline of life.

quiz.q: A dichotomous key works by offering the user
quiz.solution: At every step the key gives two mutually exclusive alternatives that progressively narrow the identification.

quiz.q: Which kingdom contains eukaryotic, multicellular, heterotrophic organisms lacking cell walls?
quiz.solution: Animals are multicellular eukaryotic heterotrophs whose cells have a flexible plasma membrane and no cell wall.

quiz.q: Nutrition in green plants is described as
quiz.solution: Green plants manufacture their own organic food from carbon dioxide and water using light energy, hence autotrophic.
